quiz.q: How does Cargo know to run a build script?
options: You register it in [build-dependencies] in Cargo.toml
It automatically compiles and runs any file named build.rs at the crate root before the rest of the build
You pass --build-script build.rs to cargo build
You call it manually from main.rs before any other code
quiz.explain: A build.rs file at the crate root (next to Cargo.toml) is found and run automatically by Cargo before the main build — no explicit wiring is needed.

quiz.q: How does a build script communicate instructions back to Cargo?
options: By writing to a file named cargo.json
By printing specially-formatted lines to stdout, like cargo::rerun-if-changed=...
By returning a special exit code for each instruction
By setting environment variables before it exits
quiz.explain: Cargo parses the build script's stdout for lines starting with the cargo:: (or legacy cargo:) prefix, treating each one as an instruction.

options: It deletes PATH before the build script runs
It tells Cargo to only re-run the build script when PATH changes, instead of on every build
It copies PATH into OUT_DIR
It sets PATH as an environment variable for the main crate
quiz.explain: Without it, Cargo's default heuristics may re-run (or fail to re-run) the script incorrectly; declaring the exact file(s) it depends on keeps rebuilds correct and fast.

quiz.q: A build script does `println!("cargo::rustc-env=GIT_HASH={}", hash)`. How does the main crate read that value at compile time?
options: std::env::var("GIT_HASH") at runtime
env!("GIT_HASH") — resolved at compile time and baked into the binary
It's automatically available as a global constant named GIT_HASH
include!("GIT_HASH")
quiz.explain: cargo::rustc-env sets a compile-time environment variable; env!("KEY") in the crate's own code reads it and bakes the value directly into the binary.

quiz.q: Why does Cargo only parse a build script's stdout, and not stderr, for instructions?
options: stderr is reserved for compiler errors only
That's just the convention — printing an instruction via eprintln! is silently ignored, shown only as plain diagnostic text
stderr output isn't captured by Cargo at all
Instructions can be printed to either stream interchangeably
quiz.explain: Only stdout lines are parsed as Cargo instructions. Anything sent to stderr is just displayed as ordinary text (e.g. with -vv), never acted on.

quiz.q: When cross-compiling, on which machine does build.rs itself actually run?
options: The target platform being compiled for
The host machine doing the compiling — never the target
Both, once for each
Neither — it runs inside a sandboxed emulator of the target
quiz.explain: build.rs is always compiled for, and executed on, the host machine, even when the crate itself is being cross-compiled for a different target.

quiz.q: Name one common real-world use of a build script.
options: Running the crate's unit tests
Generating Rust code from a schema (e.g. protobuf), compiling a bundled C library, or embedding metadata like a git commit hash
Publishing the crate to crates.io
Formatting the crate's source code
quiz.explain: Typical build.rs uses include codegen from an external schema, compiling/linking native C code (often via the `cc` crate), and stamping in build-time metadata.

quiz.q: Why is a slow or network-dependent build script a real problem?
options: It only affects the very first build, never subsequent ones
It makes every single `cargo build` slower and less reproducible, since it runs before the crate compiles
Cargo automatically caches its result forever regardless of changes
It has no real downside since it runs in parallel with compilation
quiz.explain: The build script runs before compilation on every build that triggers it, so anything slow or flaky inside it (like a network call) taxes every build and can break offline/reproducible builds.

flashcards.front: Where does a build script live, and how does Cargo find it?
flashcards.back: A file named build.rs at the crate root, next to Cargo.toml (not inside src/). Cargo automatically compiles and runs it before the rest of the crate builds — no configuration needed.

flashcards.front: How does a build script send instructions to Cargo?
flashcards.back: By printing specially-formatted lines to stdout, such as `cargo::rerun-if-changed=...` or `cargo::rustc-env=KEY=VALUE`. Cargo parses stdout for these; stderr is just shown as plain text.

flashcards.front: What does cargo::rerun-if-changed=PATH do, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: It tells Cargo to only re-run the build script when PATH changes. Omitting it risks Cargo not noticing a dependency changed and reusing stale generated output.

flashcards.front: How do you get a build-script-set value into your crate's compiled code?
flashcards.back: The build script prints `cargo::rustc-env=KEY=VALUE`; the crate's own code reads it at compile time with `env!("KEY")`, which bakes the value into the binary.

flashcards.front: On which machine does build.rs run when cross-compiling?
flashcards.back: Always the host machine doing the compiling, never the target. Reading cfg!(target_os = ...) inside build.rs reflects the host, not the target you're building for.

flashcards.front: List three common real uses of a build script.
flashcards.back: Generating Rust code from a schema (e.g. protobuf/GraphQL), compiling and linking a bundled C library (often via the `cc` crate), and embedding build metadata like a git commit hash.

flashcards.front: What's the downside of a slow or network-dependent build script?
flashcards.back: It runs before every triggered `cargo build`, so it slows down every build and can make builds flaky or non-reproducible if it depends on network access.

flashcards.front: What happens if a build script panics because required input is missing?
flashcards.back: The entire build aborts. A bare .unwrap() gives whoever hits it an unhelpful backtrace instead of a clear explanation of what was missing and why.
